passages.source_text: ὦ ἀνόητοι, ὑμεῖς τοῦ λεγομένου γενέσθε δίκαιοι κριταί. εἴπερ γὰρ καὶ ἐχρῆν ἐνταῦθα εἰς εὐφρασίαν σώματος ἑαυτὸν δοῦναι: ποία εὐωχία ἀμείνων, ἡ ἐν ποταμοῖς καὶ ὕλαις καὶ ἄλσεσιν, ἔνθα εἰλαπίναι καὶ συμπόσια καὶ κατάσκιοι τόποι, ἢ ὅπου ἀπόνοια δαιμόνων καὶ χειρῶν τομαὶ καὶ αἰδοίων ἀποκοπαὶ καὶ οἶστροι καὶ μανίαι καὶ τριχῶν καρμοὶ καὶ κόμποι καὶ ἐνθουσιασμοὶ καὶ ὀλολυγαὶ καὶ πάντα ἐκεῖνα τὰ μεθ’ ὑποκρίσεως εἰς κατάπληξιν τῶν ἀνοήτων γινόμενα, ὅπως τὰς αὐτῶν ὀφειλομένας εὐχὰς καὶ εὐχαριστίας καὶ νεκρῶν νεκροτέροις προσενέγκητε;

καὶ διὰ τί χαίροντες ταῦτα ποιεῖτε; ἐπεὶ οὐ θέλει ὑμῖν ὁ ἐμφωλεύων εἰπεῖν ὄφις, ὃς ἐνέσπειρεν ὑμῖν τὴν ἄκαρπον ἐπιθυμίαν, λέγων ὑπομνήσω. ἔχει δὲ οὕτως· παρὰ τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ θρησκείᾳ κηρύσσεται νήφειν, σωφρονεῖν, ὀργῆς κρατεῖν, ἀλλότρια μὴ νοσφίζεσθαι, δικαίως βιοῦν, ἐπιεικῶς, εὐσταθῶς, πράως, κολάζειν ἑαυτὸν μᾶλλον ἐν ταῖς ἐνδείαις ἢ μὴ ἔχοντα ἑτέρου ἀδίκως ἀφελόμενον κορεσθῆναι. παρὰ δὲ τοῖς λεγομένοις θεοῖς τὰ ἐναντία γίνεται. καὶ ἔνια εἰς κατάπληξιν δικαιοσύνης παραγγέλλεται, ἅπερ εἰ καὶ πάντα ποιεῖτε τὰ παραγγέλματα, μία ἡ πρὸς θεὸν ἄγνοια ἱκανὴ τυγχάνει πρὸς τὴν καθ’ ὑμῶν τιμωρίαν. πλὴν συνερχόμενοι εἰς τοὺς ὑφ’ ὑμῶν αὐτοῖς δοθέντας τόπους ἡδέως μεθύσκεσθε καὶ βωμοὺς ἀνάπτετε, ὧν ἡ κνίσα ῥεμβομένη καὶ τὰ τυφλὰ καὶ κωφὰ πνεύματα διὰ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἄγει εἰς τὸν τῆς ὀσφρήσεως αὐτῶν τόπον. καὶ οὕτως τῶν ἐκεῖ οἱ μὲν ἐνθουσιασμῶν, οἱ δὲ βρωτῶν ἀλλοκότων ἐμπίμπλανται, οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ ἀσελγαίνειν τρέπονται, οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ κλοπὰς καὶ φόνους. ἡ γὰρ τοῦ ἐκεῖ αἵματος ἀναθυμίασις καὶ ἡ τῶν οἴνων σπονδὴ καὶ αὐτὰ χοροῖ τὰ ἀκάθαρτα πνεύματα, ἅτινα ἐνδομυχοῦντα εἰς ὑμᾶς φιληδόνως ἔχειν τὰ ἐκεῖ ποιοῦσιν καὶ δι’ ὀνείρων ὑμᾶς φαντασίαις ψευδέσιν περιβάλλουσιν καὶ μυρίοις παθήμασιν τιμωροῦσιν. προφάσει γὰρ τῶν λεγομένων ἱεροθύτων χαλεπῶν δαιμόνων ἐμπίπλασθε, οἳ καὶ φρονίμως ὑμᾶς λανθάνοντες ἀναιροῦσιν, ἵνα μὴ συνῆτε ὑμῶν τὴν ἐπιβουλήν. προφάσει γάρ τινος ἐπηρείας ἢ ἀνάγκης ἢ ἔρωτος ἢ ὀργῆς ἢ λύπης ἢ ἀγχόνῃ ἢ ὕδατι πνίξαντες ἢ ἀπὸ κρημνοῦ ῥίψαντες ἢ αὐτοχειρίᾳ ἢ ἀποπληξίᾳ ἢ ἑτέρῳ τινὶ πάθει τοῦ ζῆν μεθιστᾶσιν.

ὅθεν ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας προφήτης πολὺ τὸν κόσμον πεπλανημένον εἰδὼς καὶ τῇ κακίᾳ συνθέμενον ἰδὼν οὐκ ἠγάπησεν τὴν πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰρήνην, ὡς ἐκ πλάνης συνοῦσαν. ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς ἀντὶ πλάνης τοῖς νήψασιν ὥσπερ πῦρ ἐμβαλὼν τὴν κατὰ τοῦ ἐνεδρεύσαντος ὀργὴν μαχαίρᾳ ἐοικυῖαν, προτείνας λόγον ἀναιρεῖ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τῇ γνώσει, ὥσπερ τέμνων καὶ χωρίζων ζῶντας ἀπὸ τῶν. νεκρῶν. τῆς μὲν οὖν κακίας ὑπὸ τῆς νομίμου γνώσεως νικωμένης πόλεμος συνεῖχε τὸ πᾶν. σωτηρίας γὰρ χάριν υἱὸς ὑπείξας ἀπειθοῦς ἐχωρίζετο πατρὸς ἢ καὶ πατὴρ τέκνου ἢ τεκοῦσα θυγατρὸς ἢ θυγάτηρ μητρὸς καὶ ἀπαξαπλῶς συγγενεῖς συγγενῶν καὶ φίλοι συνήθων.

καὶ μήτις λεγέτω Πῶς τοῦτο δίκαιον, χωρίζεσθαι γονεῖς τέκνων καὶ τέκνα γονέων; δίκαιον καὶ πάνυ. εἰ γὰρ συνόντες μετὰ τοῦ μηδὲν αὐτοὺς ὠφελεῖν καὶ συναπώλλυντο αὐτοῖς, πῶς οὐ δίκαιον καὶ χωρισθῆναι τὸν σῴζεσθαι θέλοντα ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ θέλοντος, συναπολέσθαι δὲ βουλομένου; πρὸς τούτοις οὐδὲ αὐτοὶ οἱ τὸ κρεῖττον νενοηκότες χωρισθῆναι ἤθελον, ἀλλὰ συνεῖναι καὶ ὠφελεῖν αὐτοὺς τῇ τῶν κρειττόνων ὑφηγήσει, ὅθεν οἱ ἀπειθεῖς ἐπακούειν αὐτῶν μὴ θέλοντες αὐτοὶ αὐτοὺς ἐπολέμουν, χωρίζοντες, διώκοντες, μισοῦντες. οἱ δὲ ταῦτα πάσχοντες, ἐλεῶντες αὐτοὺς ὑπὸ ἀγνοίας ἐνεδρευομένους, διδασκαλίᾳ φρονήσεως ηὔχοντο ὑπὲρ τῶν τὰ κακὰ αὐτοὺς διατιθεμένων, τὴν ἄγνοιαν τοῦ ἁμαρτήματος αἰτίαν εἶναι μεμαθηκότες. αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ διδάσκαλος προσηλωθεὶς ηὔχετο τῷ πατρὶ τοῖς αὐτὸν ἀναιροῦσιν ἀφεθῆναι τὸ ἁμάρτημα εἰπὼν „πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν, οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν ἃ ποιοῦσιν“. μιμηταὶ οὖν γινόμενοι τοῦ διδασκάλου καὶ αὐτοί, ἐν οἷς ἔπασχον ὑπὲρ τῶν διατιθεμένων ηὔχοντο ὡς ἐδιδάχθησαν. οὕτως οὐ γονεῖς μισοῦντες ἐχωρίζο[ντο], ὁπότε καὶ ὑπὲρ τῶν μὴ γονέων μ[ὲν ὄντ]ων, ἐχθρῶν δὲ γενομένων ἐποιοῦντ[ο τὰς] εὐχὰς καὶ ἀγαπᾶν πειρῶνται ὡς ἐκελεύσθησαν.

εἴπατε δέ μοι ὑμεῖς πῶς τοὺς γονεῖς ἀγαπᾶτε; εἰ μὲν ὡς τὸ δίκαιον ἀεὶ σκοποῦντες, συνεύχομαι· εἰ δὲ ὡς ἔτυχεν, οὐκέτι· δύνασθε γὰρ καὶ μικρᾷ προφάσει τούτων γενέσθαι ἐχθροί. εἰ δὲ εἰδότες ἀγαπᾶτε, εἴπατε ἡμῖν τί ἐστιν „γονεῖς“. ἐρεῖτε Γένους ἀρχηγέται. διὰ τί οὖν τὸ τῶν ὅλων γένος οὐχ ἠγαπήσατε, εἴπερ δικαίῳ φρονήματι τοῦτο ποιεῖν ἐπανείλεσθε; ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐρεῖτε Οὐχ ἑωράκαμεν αὐτόν. διὰ τί οὖν μὴ ζητήσαντες τὰ ἀναίσθητα κολακεύετε; τί δέ; εἰ καὶ δύσκολον ἦν ὑμῖν γνῶναι τί θεός, τὸ μέντοι τί οὐ θεὸς μὴ εἰδέναι οὐκ ἐδύνασθε, ἵνα λογίσησθε ὅτι θεός ἐστιν οὐ ξύλον, οὐ λίθος, οὐ χαλκός, οὐχ ἄλλο τι ἐκ φθαρτῆς γεγονὸς ὕλης.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.
context.selected_edition_coverage_standard: Coverage is assessed against ALL SURVIVING WORDING AND PRINTED GAP MARKERS in the selected image-checked edition, not against unavailable words of a hypothetical complete original. A confirmed printed lacuna must remain an explicit gap in the English, retaining the exact number of printed dots (layout whitespace may differ), with a source-quoted note explaining that its content is unavailable and no restoration has been supplied. Such faithful representation can pass selected-edition coverage; it must never be described as recovery of the lost wording or an unbroken original. Distinguish this from missing scan pages, unverified ink, omitted surviving Greek, an unsupported English completion, or a translation that obscures the gap: those remain blocking. Neither this scope clarification nor a prior suggestion is an instruction to accept a draft; independently check every surviving clause, every gap, and every disclosure.

passages.text: Senseless people, become just judges of what is being said. For even if one ought to give oneself over to bodily enjoyment here, which feast is better: one by rivers and woods and groves, where there are banquets and drinking parties and shaded places, or one where there is the frenzy of demons, cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals, fits of fury and madness, clipping of hair, boasts, possession, shrieks, and all those things done theatrically to astound the senseless, so that you offer their owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?

lexical_decisions.chosen: cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both named ritual injuries soberly without euphemism or added detail.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to things deader even than the dead
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the pointed comparative and its rhetorical excess.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως τὰς αὐτῶν ὀφειλομένας εὐχὰς καὶ εὐχαριστίας καὶ νεκρῶν νεκροτέροις προσενέγκητε;
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that you offer their owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their preserves the printed third-person αὐτῶν alongside second-person you offer. It can refer to the previously mentioned senseless people, potentially including the audience. Your is a contextual identification alternative, but the main text does not silently harmonize the pronouns.

passages.text: And why do you do these things gladly? Since the serpent nesting within you, who sowed fruitless desire in you, does not want to tell you, I will remind you by explaining. It is like this: in the worship of God it is proclaimed that one must be clear-minded, exercise self-control, master anger, not appropriate what belongs to others, live justly, reasonably, steadily, and gently, and discipline oneself in deprivation rather than, when lacking something, take it unjustly from someone else and be filled. But among the so-called gods, the opposite happens. Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness; yet even if you perform all the commands, ignorance of God alone is sufficient for your punishment. Nevertheless, you gather at the places you have assigned to them, gladly become drunk, and kindle altars. Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through the power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it. Thus, of those there, some are filled with possession, others with strange foods, while others turn to shameless conduct and others to thefts and murders. For the vapor of the blood there and the libation of wines set even the impure spirits themselves dancing. Lurking within you, they make you take pleasure in what goes on there, surround you through dreams with false visions, and punish you with countless afflictions. For under the pretext of the so-called sacrificial offerings you are filled with fierce demons, who also kill you while cunningly escaping your notice, so that you do not understand the plot against you. For under the pretext of some abuse, necessity, passion, anger, or grief, they remove you from life by hanging, by drowning you in water, by throwing you from a cliff, by your own hand, by a stroke, or by some other affliction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἔνια εἰς κατάπληξιν δικαιοσύνης παραγγέλλεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase relates certain commands to an impressive effect associated with righteousness. An impressive display of righteousness is another viable rendering; the main text does not decide that all such commands are merely fraudulent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ κνίσα ῥεμβομένη καὶ τὰ τυφλὰ καὶ κωφὰ πνεύματα διὰ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἄγει εἰς τὸν τῆς ὀσφρήσεως αὐτῶν τόπον.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through the power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Smoke is the grammatical subject, but the possessor or source of ἐξουσία is not stated. The power leaves it unspecified. Its power, assigning power to the smoke, is a defensible contextual alternative, not an explicit Greek possessive. No divine or demonic source of the power is independently added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: set even the impure spirits themselves dancing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the dancing image, not merely attraction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by your own hand, by a stroke
lexical_decisions.rationale: By your own hand understands the demons as inducing the victims’ self-killing, supported by the listed pretexts and means of death. αὐτοχειρία can also be killing with one’s own hand, so direct killing by the demons themselves is a material alternative given the surrounding demonic subjects. Stroke preserves the separate ἀποπληξία without adding clinical detail.

passages.text: Therefore the prophet of truth, knowing that the world was greatly deceived and seeing that it had agreed with evil, did not love peace with it, since that peace arose from error. Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil, in place of error he cast into those who had become clear-minded an anger against the one who had ambushed them, like fire and resembling a sword. Holding out the word, he does away with ignorance through knowledge, as though cutting and separating the living from the dead. So, as evil was overcome by knowledge in accordance with the law, war gripped everything. For the sake of salvation a son who yielded separated from a disobedient father, or a father from a child, or a mother from a daughter, or a daughter from a mother—in short, relatives from relatives and friends from companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object brought is implicit. Death is inferred from the end of 11.18 and the ensuing living/dead contrast. The it can be the peace founded on error or its sustaining error; no new punishment is specified.
The recipient of yielding is not explicit. The saving instruction is contextual, but the English does not insert that recipient.

passages.text: And let no one say, “How is this just, for parents to be separated from children and children from parents?” It is entirely just. For if by staying with them they not only did them no good but also perished with them, how is it not just for the one who wants to be saved to be separated from the one who does not want to be saved but wants to perish together? Moreover, those who had understood what is better did not themselves want to be separated, but to remain with them and benefit them by teaching better things. Therefore the disobedient, unwilling to listen to them, themselves fought against them, separating them, persecuting them, and hating them. But those who suffered these things pitied them as people ambushed by ignorance and, taught to understand, prayed for those who mistreated them, having learned that ignorance is the cause of sin. For the teacher himself, when nailed up, prayed to the Father that the sin of those killing him might be forgiven, saying, “Father, forgive them their sins, for they do not know what they are doing.” Becoming imitators of the teacher themselves, in their sufferings they prayed for those who inflicted them, as they had been taught. Thus they did not separate because they hated their parents, since they even offered prayers for those who were not their parents but had become enemies, and try to love them as they were commanded.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative connects instruction in understanding with the prayerful response, not with a newly supplied revelation.
Bracketed letters are already supplied by the selected edition; no new restoration has been made.
Follows the supplied bracketed reading and preserves the contrast with enemies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ θέλοντος, συναπολέσθαι δὲ βουλομένου;
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the one who does not want to be saved but wants to perish together?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person described by βουλομένου remains the subject of co-perishing. To be saved repeats the contextual object of willing in the prior clause, not a new wish for other people’s destruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν οἱ ἀπειθεῖς ἐπακούειν αὐτῶν μὴ θέλοντες αὐτοὶ αὐτοὺς ἐπολέμουν, χωρίζοντες, διώκοντες, μισοῦντες.
lexical_decisions.chosen: themselves fought against them, separating them, persecuting them, and hating them.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expressed αὐτούς is taken as the shared object of the parallel participles, giving the disobedient people agency in imposing separation. Separating from them is an intransitive alternative, but it is less source-transparent after the statement that the instructed people did not want separation.

passages.text: But tell me: how do you love your parents? If you do so with a constant regard for what is just, I join in your prayer; but if merely as it happens, I do not, for even on a small pretext you can become their enemies. If you love with knowledge, tell us what “parents” means. You will say, “Founders of a family line.” Why, then, have you not loved the origin of all things, if you have undertaken to do this with a just mind? But even now you will say, “We have not seen him.” Why, then, do you flatter insensible things without having searched? And what of this? Even if it was difficult for you to know what God is, you could not fail to know what is not God, so that you might reason that God is not wood, not stone, not bronze, or anything else made of perishable matter.

lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος links the argument to lineage and parentage. Origin or source here refers to God; progenitor of all is a viable more explicitly personal alternative.
Retains the prayer compound; join in wishing this is also possible, rather than bare agreement.
Preserves the separate rhetorical question introducing the final argument.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
